title: Tiny Teeth Reveal Our First Primate Ancestor Spread Farther Than Thought
hook: Fossil teeth smaller than a fingertip just pushed the known range of Purgatorius — the earliest relative of every primate, including us — hundreds of miles south.
key_points: Purgatorius is the earliest-known relative of all primates, including humans.
New tooth fossils found in Colorado's Denver Basin mark the southernmost Purgatorius remains yet discovered.
It was previously thought to be confined to Montana and parts of Canada.
The shrew-sized, tree-dwelling animal appears to have spread south soon after the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs.
content_html: Some of the most important fossils in primate evolution are barely visible to the naked eye. Paleontologists have found tooth-sized remains of Purgatorius — the earliest-known relative of all primates, including humans — in Colorado's Denver Basin, as ScienceDaily reports.
extra_html: Purgatorius was a shrew-sized, tree-dwelling mammal that lived in the immediate aftermath of the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs. Until now, its known range was thought to be limited to Montana and parts of Canada. The new Colorado teeth are the southernmost Purgatorius remains found to date, suggesting this tiny animal spread across a much wider swath of North America, and did so quickly, in the scramble to fill ecological niches left empty by the extinction. It's a reminder that the primate story — and by extension, our own — starts not in a lush jungle but in the chaotic recovery period after a mass extinction.

related.title: The First Primates May Have Started in the Cold
related.hook: We picture our primate ancestors in steamy jungles. A new study suggests the earliest ones may instead have arisen in cold, dry North America — some perhaps even hibernating.

related.title: Human Evolution
related.hook: We didn't descend from chimpanzees — we share an ancestor with them. From that branching point, our lineage walked upright, grew big brains, and spread across the planet.

related.title: Mass Extinctions
related.hook: Five times in the past half-billion years, life on Earth was nearly wiped out. Each catastrophe reset the course of evolution — and the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs was only the most famous.

flashcards.back_html: It's the earliest-known relative of all primates, including humans — a shrew-sized, tree-dwelling animal from just after the dinosaurs' extinction.

flashcards.prompt: What did the new Colorado fossils change about Purgatorius's known range?

choices.text: They extended it far south, beyond the previously known Montana/Canada range
They proved Purgatorius never left South America
They showed Purgatorius lived only underwater

flashcards.explanation_html: Purgatorius was thought confined to Montana and parts of Canada; the Denver Basin teeth are the southernmost remains found so far.

flashcards.prompt: When does Purgatorius appear to have spread across this wider range?

Tens of millions of years before the dinosaurs existed
